land.text: the former Duchy of Luxembourg, 'restored' by the Congress of Vienna after Napoleon's defeat and raised to a Grand Duchy

predecessors.note: The page names no previous holder; the French Empire is the researcher's inference from 'After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815'. The Duchy of Luxembourg dossier (duchy-of-luxembourg) ends in 1443 and is a different state 450 years earlier.

capitals.name: Luxembourg City
capitals.note: 'Its capital and most populous city, Luxembourg City'; the fortress was manned by Prussian troops under the German Confederation until 1867.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1815-1829: Cliopatria's row starts in 1890. The Congress of Vienna decided 'to restore the Duchy of Luxembourg' as a Grand Duchy in personal union with the Netherlands. The original duchy of 10,700 km2 had lost 1,060 km2 to France in 1659 and, at the Congress, 2,280 km2 to Prussia ('24% of Luxembourg's contemporary area'); the Belgium province ceded in 1839 was 4,730 km2, 'or 65% of the territory of the Grand Duchy at the time', which makes the Grand Duchy of 1815-1830 about 7,300 km2: today's Luxembourg (2,586 km2) plus the Belgian province.

correction.text: the Grand Duchy of 1815: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg (Arlon, Bastogne, Virton, Neufchateau), about 7,300 km2

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1830-1838: 'At the outbreak of the Belgian Revolution, most Luxembourgers joined the Belgian rebels and took control of most of the Grand Duchy'; Belgium 'claimed the entire Grand-Duchy of Luxembourg as part of Belgium' and the Dutch king and Prussia rejected the claim. What the Grand Duchy held is the capital and its fortress (the Belgium dossier cites 'Only Luxembourg City ... stayed out of Belgian hands'); the rest is the contested zone of the ledger (drawn blended).

correction.text: Luxembourg City and its fortress, the only part not held by the Belgian rebels

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1839-1889: after the Treaty of London the Grand Duchy is the German-speaking rump: 'The partitions reduced the territory of Luxembourg from 10,700 km2 to the present-day area of 2,586 km2'; Belgium received 4,730 km2, 'or 65% of the territory of the Grand Duchy at the time', with Arlon, Bastogne, Virton and Neufchateau. The shape is the 1890 one. It stayed in personal union with the Netherlands until 1890, joined the Zollverein in 1842, and its independence and neutrality were reaffirmed by the Second Treaty of London (1867).

correction.text: the rump Grand Duchy, 2,586 km2 on the page

keyframe_review.note: 2405 km2 for 1890: the same 11 H3 cells as the 1890 shape (+-1 cell of border rounding), against 2,586 km2 on the page (ratio 0.93). No frontier change. This is the first Cliopatria year: the Dutch monarchy 'ceased to hold the title Grand-Duke of Luxembourg' and the country has its own monarchy under Adolph of Nassau-Weilburg; the shape also stands for 1891-1914.

New keyframe 1915-1918: Cliopatria has no Luxembourg shape in these years (the German Empire shape of 1915-1917 contains the 20 Luxembourg cells). The page: 'the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg was under full occupation by the German Empire' but 'was allowed to retain its own government and political system'. The land stays Luxembourg's, drawn hatched by the occupation events.

The German withdrawal was completed on 22 November 1918; American and French troops filled the vacuum, and the September 1919 referendum 'found 77.8% in favour of continued rule by the House of Nassau-Weilburg'.

'On 10 May 1940, the German Wehrmacht invaded Luxembourg' and the country was 'finally annexed directly into Germany' (Gau Moselland); the government and Grand Duchess Charlotte went into exile. The land stays Luxembourg's (hatched, then German-annexed in the ledger).

ledger.note: 1815: the Congress of Vienna creates the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. 'After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815, the Congress of Vienna decided to restore the Duchy of Luxembourg'; raised to a Grand Duchy, it 'would be joined with the Netherlands in personal union under King William I' and 'would become a member state of the newly formed German Confederation'. The page gives no day; the Netherlands dossier dates the Dutch acquisition to May 1815.

region.text: the restored Duchy raised to a Grand Duchy: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

ledger.note: 1815: Prussia receives the north-eastern Eifel part of the duchy. 'The Second Partition reduced Luxembourg's territory by 2,280 km2, or 24% of Luxembourg's contemporary area'; 'Along with Bitburg, Prussia gained the towns of Neuerburg, Sankt Vith, Schleiden and Waxweiler' (infobox: 'Lost to Prussia by the Congress of Vienna in 1815'). The keyframe of 1815 is already net of this cession.

region.text: Bitburg, Neuerburg, Sankt Vith, Schleiden and Waxweiler, about 2,280 km2 (the circles are three radii around Bitburg, Sankt Vith and Schleiden; the gazetteer lacks the names)

ledger.note: 1830: the Belgian revolt takes most of the Grand Duchy. 'At the outbreak of the Belgian Revolution, most Luxembourgers joined the Belgian rebels and took control of most of the Grand Duchy'; Luxembourg City, the fortress, stays out. Year not on the page (the Belgium and Netherlands dossiers date it 1830); the region copies the Belgium dossier's gain.

region.text: the Grand Duchy without Luxembourg City: the countryside and the Belgian province held by the rebels

ledger.note: 1839: the German-speaking rump returns to the Grand Duke. 'The largest territorial loss occurred under the 1839 Treaty of London': Belgium received 4,730 km2 ('65% of the territory of the Grand Duchy at the time', 175,000 people: Arlon, Bastogne, Virton, Neufchateau); the LUX page: the treaty 'also established full independence of the remaining Germanic-speaking Grand-Duchy'. The page gives no day (the Belgium and Netherlands dossiers say 19 April 1839). The Belgian province is lost in law here and already lost in fact since 1830.

region.text: the remaining Germanic-speaking Grand Duchy, 2,586 km2

ledger.note: 1890: the personal union with the Netherlands ends and a new dynasty takes the throne. A succession crisis: 'the Dutch monarchy ceased to hold the title Grand-Duke of Luxembourg', and under 'Adolph of Nassau-Weilburg, the Grand-Duchy would have its own monarchy'. Same state, new house (Orange-Nassau to Nassau-Weilburg); Cliopatria's Luxembourg row starts here.

2 August 1914: Germany occupies Luxembourg without a fight. 'the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg was under full occupation by the German Empire' from 2 August; Marie-Adelaide 'ordered the small army not to resist'; the country 'was allowed to retain its own government and political system'.

22 November 1918: the last German troops leave. 'On 22 November 1918, the German army completed its withdrawal from Luxembourg, ending its occupation'; von Tessmar had announced the withdrawal on 6 November and Germany signed the armistice five days later.

10 May 1940: the Wehrmacht invades. 'On 10 May 1940, the German Wehrmacht invaded Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands'; a military administration was set up 'the following day' and Gustav Simon became head of the civil administration on 21 July 1940.

1942: the occupation becomes annexation. The page says only that the country 'was finally annexed directly into Germany' (Gau Moselland) with no date; the nazi-germany dossier dates the annexation to August 1942 from the Territorial evolution of Germany page.
1942: Germany annexes Luxembourg (page silent on the date; August 1942 in the nazi-germany dossier). Luxembourg is 'annexed to the adjacent province of Nazi Germany, Gau Moselland' (Luxembourg page).

10 September 1944: American troops liberate Luxembourg City. 'The first U.S. forces entered Luxembourgish territory near Petange on 9 September, and liberated the capital city on 10 September 1944'; 'By 12 September' 90% of the Grand Duchy was free; liberation 'was not completed until early 1945' because of the Ardennes Offensive. The nazi-germany dossier closes its claim in February 1945.

zones.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, claimed in full by Belgium

wars.outcome: Belgium took most of the Grand Duchy in 1830; the Treaty of London (1839) gave Belgium 4,730 km2 (65%) and left the German-speaking rump to the Grand Duke.
wars.note: The page dates the Great Powers' relenting to July 1831 and has two dates for the treaty (1831 and 1839); Luxembourg City held out throughout.

wars.name: German invasion of Luxembourg in World War I
wars.outcome: Occupation from 2 August to 22 November 1918 with Luxembourg's government kept; no change of frontier.

wars.name: German invasion of Luxembourg in World War II
wars.outcome: Occupied from 10 May 1940 and annexed to Gau Moselland; liberated from 9 September 1944, with the Ardennes offensive delaying the end to early 1945.

certainty.note: The Grand Duchy's frontier with the Netherlands' southern provinces and the Belgian rebels was disputed after 1830; the 1815 line is a Congress of Vienna line.
Treaty frontiers: the Treaty of London of 1839, confirmed by the Second Treaty of London in 1867; the 1919 and 1945 frontiers are unchanged.

notes: One state or two: Cliopatria's Luxembourg (1890-2024, 11 cells) shares Wikidata Q2719360 with the Duchy of Luxembourg (1429-1449, 45 cells). They are different states: the duchy's dossier (duchy-of-luxembourg) already ends in 1443 under Burgundy and says no merge is made; the Grand Duchy of 1815 is a new creation of the Congress of Vienna that restored the title, 372 years later. No merge is made here and cliopatria_names has only 'Luxembourg'. Dossier years: Cliopatria starts in 1890 but the netherlands and kingdom-of-belgium dossiers already use the slug 'luxembourg' for the Grand Duchy from 1815 (vassal_start 1815, belgium gain 1830, loss 1839), so this dossier starts in 1815 with new keyframes for 1815-1889 and for the two occupations (1915-1918, 1940-1944) in which Cliopatria has no Luxembourg shape. Cliopatria's Netherlands shape may also contain Luxembourg in 1815-1889 (not checked; a compile conflict to look for). Cell checks: the ten Cliopatria shapes are the same 10-11 cells; the area differences (2,249 to 2,405 km2) are border rounding. Page silent: day dates of the Congress of Vienna and the 1839 treaty; the list of grand dukes (no rulers strip: the page gives no reign years); the exact annexation date of 1942. Gazetteer names needed: Bitburg, Neuerburg, Sankt Vith, Schleiden, Waxweiler (3 coordinate circles used). Counterpart first-french-empire is an inference (the page does not name the previous holder). Not researched (budget): Luxembourg's role in the Zollverein (1842-1918), BLEU 1921 and the Benelux, which move no frontier.
